stem: A nurse is preparing to administer a hazardous antineoplastic drug for which a protective gown is required. Which gown characteristic is most appropriate?

options.A: A disposable protective gown made of a nonabsorbent barrier material, with long sleeves and tight-fitting cuffs
options.B: A cloth laboratory coat because absorbent fabric is preferred for hazardous-drug splashes
options.C: A standard short-sleeved isolation garment because chemotherapy gloves alone protect the forearms
options.D: A previously used hazardous-drug gown that is dry and has no visible contamination

rationale: OSHA hazardous-drug guidance states that protective gowns should not have seams or closures that allow drugs to pass through and should have long sleeves with tight-fitting cuffs. Disposable polyethylene-coated polypropylene or other laminate materials provide better protection than non-coated absorbent materials. Gowns should be disposed of after each use rather than reused. OSHA also notes that there is no single specific performance standard requiring gowns to be labeled 'chemotherapy-tested.' Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Select appropriate hazardous-drug protective gowns: use a disposable, nonabsorbent barrier garment with long sleeves and tight cuffs, and do not reuse contaminated or previously worn gowns.
source_organization: U.S. Department of Labor — Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
source_document_title: Hazardous Drugs — Controlling Occupational Exposure to Hazardous Drugs
source_locator: Personal Protective Equipment → Gowns: gowns should not have seams/closures allowing drug passage; should have long sleeves with tight-fitting cuffs; disposable polyethylene-coated polypropylene or other laminate materials offer better protection than non-coated materials; cloth lab coats/scrubs are absorbent; dispose of gowns after each use; OSHA notes no specific gown standard for chemotherapy-drug permeation testing
source_claim_supported: Hazardous-drug gowns should provide a nonabsorbent protective barrier with long sleeves/tight cuffs and should not be reused; a universal 'chemotherapy-tested gown' designation is not required by a single specific performance standard.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Handling Hazardous and Infectious Materials, printed p.25 / PDF p.29: follow procedures for handling biohazardous and hazardous materials; demonstrate safe handling techniques
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hazardous-drug PPE / protective gown selection
correction_summary: Removed the unsupported requirement that a hazardous-drug gown must be specifically 'rated/tested for chemotherapy drug protection.' Replaced it with current OSHA-supported barrier, sleeve, cuff, material, and single-use characteristics.
audit_findings: A matches OSHA's gown characteristics. B uses absorbent material that can retain hazardous drugs against skin. C leaves forearms insufficiently protected and incorrectly assumes gloves replace gown protection. D conflicts with the recommendation to dispose of gowns after each use. The revised answer avoids inventing an ASTM chemotherapy-gown performance requirement that OSHA explicitly says is not established. NCSBN 2026 mapping is direct; independent second pass found one best answer.
